newsitem.title: UK: Lira takes heart from EU deficit footnote.
newsitem.headline: Lira takes heart from EU deficit footnote.

text.p: The lira retreated after the European Union predicted Italy's deficit would exceed 3.0 percent of GDP in 1997/98, but advanced again on suggestions it could hit the key EMU goal if existing and new measures work.

"...this (3.2 percent) may become 3.0 percent of GDP for 1997, if the measures already taken have full effectiveness and, if necessary, additional measures are introduced," the European Commission said in a footnote to its economic forecasts.
The Commission foresaw only Italy and Greece overshooting 3.0 percent, predicting the Italian budget shortfall at 3.2 percent of GDP this year and 3.9 in 1998.

The lira was trading at 994.50/80 per mark at 1011 GMT. It sank from late Tuesday's level of 995.50/90 to a low of 997.95 in morning Europe, though had clawed back to around 995.60 just before the EU forecasts appeared.

"They (the Commission) seem to be saying they're not convinced all the mini-budget measures will be effective, but if they are it'll be 3.0 rather than 3.2 percent," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase Investment Bank in London.
The Italian government's proposed mini-budget was rejected by a parliamentary commission last week, raising the prospect of a confidence vote.
The mini-budget was dealt a further blow at the weekend when the International Monetary Fund criticised it, saying it stressed EMU aspirations at the expense of structural reform.

Gunner said the 3.9 percent forecast for 1998 reflected a sense Italy is not sustaining economic improvement, and that appeared negative for the lira. But the forecast took no account of the 1998 budget, which could tighten fiscal policy sufficiently to hit the 3.0 percent target, he added.
Economists said, however, that the diplomatic pressure to push down Italy's 1997 deficit figure had clearly failed, emphasising the Commission's doubts on Italy.
The Commission predicted that Germany, France, Spain and Portugal would record budget deficits of 3.0 percent of GDP this year.

"It is conspicuous that the Commission's forecasts for a lot of EU countries are exactly at 3.0 percent. The Commission's forecast for Germany is the most optimistic of all possibilities," said Holger Fahrinkrug, senior economist at UBS in Frankfurt.
Fahrinkrug, whose own forecast was 3.4 percent, said 3.0 percent was theoretically possible, but not without a tax increase and/or further substantial savings efforts.
Austria's 1997 shortfall was estimated at 3.0 percent, with Britain on 2.9, Belgium 2.7, Sweden at 2.6, the Netherlands on 2.3, Finland 1.9, Ireland at 1.0, but Greece seen at 4.9.
Denmark and Luxembourg would be in surplus, the EU said.

European monetary affairs commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said 13 EU states would meet the deficit target for EMU in 1997, and predicted that a majority of countries would participate in the euro's launch in 1999.
Postponement of currency union was legally and practically impossible, de Silguy told a committee of the European Parliament.
Reaction to the EU forecasts, which had been widely leaked, was mostly muted, with the mark remaining mostly a touch softer on the crosses and subdued by a firm dollar.
The mark stood at 3.3727/37 French francs and 84.39/41 pesetas at 1103 GMT versus 3.3755/59 and 84.46 late on Tuesday.
The franc was supported by an opinion poll -- the first since France's snap election was called on Monday -- indicating the centre-right would retain power.
Market fears that the Socialists, hostile to further austerity measures aimed at hitting EMU targets, have weighed on the French currency recently.
Chase's Gunner said the EMU jitters generated by the May 25/June 1 French election would continue to cap the franc's European stablemates -- chiefly the lira -- for now.
"For the rally we're seeing now (in the lira) to go much further will depend on what happens in the French elections," he said. "They will remain the centre of attention."
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
